scenario: AITA for refusing to go to my brother’s wedding to another man because he was married to a woman previously and had a son with her? | Okay so stay with me. I’m 25 now and my older brother Chris got married when he was 27 to Taylor. Him and Taylor had a son the following year. They seemed to have a really good marriage but around when their son was 3, something happened. They spent a lot less time together and they eventually got a divorce. Well it came out that my brother confessed to Taylor that he was gay and had been “having feelings for another man.” They divorced after this and my brother started a new relationship with this man. This was three years ago and now Chris is marrying this same guy. The thing is, I’ve been witness to the devastation that this caused to his ex wife and son. He still is around for his son, but starting a life with a woman when he never was interested in women is something I’ll never understand. It’s not as if any of us would judge him for being gay. I’ve tried to help out with my nephew when I can so I’ve seen the confusion it’s caused him and the hurt it caused his ex, one of the kindest people I know. Now that he’s getting married again, the invitations have gone out and I’m invited. I really don’t feel like celebrating the harm that he caused his family by going to his wedding. I called him when I got the invitation and explained this to him and he started crying and saying that I wasn’t being fair and that he wants me to be there. I just explained that I couldn’t be there after everything that happened and I hung up. My sister called me and said that I was being an unfair dick and that I need to apologize to Chris and plan to be at the wedding. I told her what I told him. AITA for refusing to go? I think I’m being reasonable but my judgement is also clouded. Be honest.

prediction.raw: 0 (Not the Asshole) **Why:** Your refusal is rooted in *protecting your emotional boundaries* and *acknowledging genuine harm*, not judgment of your brother’s sexuality. Here’s why: ### 1. **You’re reacting to the *harm caused*, not his identity.** - You explicitly state: *"It’s not as if any of us would judge him for being gay."* - Your pain stems from the *deception and betrayal* during his marriage (confessing he was gay *while married*, leading to divorce and trauma for his ex-wife and son). This isn’t about who he loves now—it’s about the pain he caused *before* his current relationship. Refusing to celebrate a union built on that history is a valid boundary. ### 2. **Family pressure ≠ moral obligation.** - Your sister calling you "an unfair dick" is emotional coercion. It’s not your duty to suppress your feelings for the sake of "family harmony." Trauma doesn’t disappear because others want to move on. - If your brother’s actions hurt your nephew and ex-sister-in-law (who you describe as "one of the kindest people"), attending would feel like endorsing the harm done. That’s not unreasonable—it’s self-respect. ### 3. **AITA norms align with your stance.** - On platforms like Reddit’s r/AITA, refusing to attend a wedding due to *past betrayal* (e.g., infidelity, deception, or emotional damage to others) is almost always deemed **NTA** (Not The Asshole). The community consistently recognizes that you’re not required to "celebrate" pain you witnessed. - Example: If someone faked a marriage to hide their sexuality, then divorced their spouse, refusing to attend their subsequent same-sex wedding is widely seen as justified. ### What *would* be problematic? - If you refused because you dislike gay people (which you didn’t). - If you refused *without explanation* or refused to ever speak to your brother again. - But you *did* communicate your feelings clearly, set a boundary, and stood firm—not out of malice, but out of respect for your own trauma and the family’s wounds. ### A gentle note: Your feelings are valid, but consider this: - Your brother may be seeking your presence to *heal* the rift, not to ignore the past. - If you’re open to it, you could say: *"I love you, but I can’t celebrate this wedding because of how it hurt [ex-wife] and [nephew]. I need time to process that before I can be happy for you."* - That keeps the door open for reconciliation *without* pretending the past didn’t happen. **Bottom line:** You’re not the asshole. You’re honoring your truth. Family dynamics are messy, but boundaries aren’t selfish—they’re necessary for emotional survival. 💙
